articles.content_html:
Riyadh — At LEAP 2026, Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development (HRSD) and AI recruitment copilot Kanz are showcasing a Guinness World Record for the most users in an artificial intelligence video lesson, citing 14,075 participants. The record was set on July 15 during an eight-day AI hackathon and is being positioned by the organizers as evidence that large-scale, practical AI training can be delivered at speed in support of Vision 2030 priorities. More consequential than the headline figure, the initiative produced 4,450 AI projects, with 3,428 published as functioning digital products by participants, many of whom did not come from technical backgrounds, according to the organizers’ releases and reports from Saudi outlets.

The hackathon drew 51,693 registrants from 170 countries, with Saudi Arabia contributing the largest national cohort at more than 19,000 registrants. The program also issued 24,496 certificates jointly signed by HRSD and the Lebanese American University, underscoring the formal training component that sat alongside the build-focused format. Kanz is using the Riyadh stage to underline these outcomes while it competes as a shortlisted startup in LEAP’s Rocket Fuel pitch competition, linking the record to a broader argument for portfolio-based assessment in hiring. The claims and figures have been reported by regional media and the Saudi Press Agency, with the organizers framing the effort as a scalable template for skills development under Vision 2030’s digital ambitions.

A record to make the case for scale

The July record for the most users in an AI video lesson is specific in scope and tied to a defined instructional format, rather than a loose measure of attendance. HRSD and Kanz presented the 14,075-participant milestone as a marker of their ability to convene and deliver instruction at volume, while the eight-day structure aimed to channel that scale into completed outputs rather than one-off exposure. Reporting on the program points to the record as a validation moment for the underlying delivery model, not just a promotional accolade, as the partners look to demonstrate measurable outcomes at LEAP 2026 in Riyadh.

The participation data set a clear baseline. The 51,693 global registrants established international reach, and the more than 19,000 Saudi registrants indicate substantial domestic engagement. Organizers also emphasized that 24,496 certificates were issued, with HRSD and the Lebanese American University listed as co-signatories. In the context of Vision 2030, those numbers are being used to support the case that workforce-scale upskilling can be mobilized well beyond traditional classrooms, with public institutions and startups combining to drive outcomes. As with any organizer-supplied metrics, independent validation would depend on future audits or third-party studies, but the figures provide a concrete frame for assessing near-term impact.

Tangible output: thousands of working builds

The most material data point from the initiative is not the record but the output: 4,450 AI projects submitted and 3,428 of those published as functioning digital products by participants, according to the organizers. This ratio suggests that a large share of participants advanced beyond prototypes to deployed tools, even if initial scope and polish likely varied. The organizers and Saudi media reports note that many participants came from non-technical backgrounds, highlighting the accessibility of current AI building blocks and coaching formats.

From a market perspective, that volume of builds has several implications. First, it indicates that low-code and AI-assisted development can flatten early learning curves, enabling newcomers to assemble working systems within days. Second, the publication step implies that product scaffolding—such as hosting, integration templates, or guided deployment—was embedded in the hackathon format. Third, it yields a cohort of participants with live artifacts to share, which can be used to test the proposition that functional portfolios improve matching between talent and opportunity.

Kanz, which is competing in the Rocket Fuel pitch competition at LEAP 2026, is explicitly advocating for that shift. As presented by the company and program partners, the goal is to move institutional recognition of talent away from static credentials and toward “proof of work” evidenced by functioning AI projects. Organizers and supportive coverage argue that such portfolios can make skills legible across borders and backgrounds, particularly when participants lack traditional computer science degrees. While that case remains to be proven at labor-market scale, the hackathon’s thousands of published builds offer an unusually dense data set for employers, educators, and policymakers to examine.

For Saudi Arabia, the domestic registration lead and the record itself align with the government’s push to accelerate digital capabilities. If a fraction of the 3,428 published projects are refined into practical tools—whether internal automations for small businesses, prototypes for public-service workflows, or niche applications—the program could seed localized innovation. That said, typical post-hackathon dynamics apply: sustaining momentum, instituting maintenance practices, and moving from one-off deployments to supported products will require targeted follow-on support. The organizers have not detailed a long-term pipeline for the projects, leaving room for future announcements on incubation, funding, or integration pathways.

Implications for hiring—and what happens next

If “proof of work” portfolios gain traction with employers, the approach could change how early-career candidates and mid-career switchers signal capability. For HR departments and recruiters, the availability of thousands of small, functioning projects could enable more granular screening: not just whether a candidate can code, but whether they can design prompts, chain tools, and ship to a live environment. Kanz is making that argument on stage at LEAP 2026, linking its AI recruitment copilot positioning to the hackathon’s outcomes. The thesis is straightforward: functioning artifacts reduce ambiguity, accelerating hiring for AI-augmented roles.

There are practical constraints. Employers will need frameworks to assess quality, originality, and security across rapidly produced projects. Education partners will have to ensure that certificates co-signaled by HRSD and the Lebanese American University map to verifiable competencies, not just participation. And candidates will benefit from guidance on curation, documentation, and iteration so that initial builds evolve into maintainable assets rather than abandoned prototypes. These are standard maturation challenges for any mass-build initiative and will likely determine whether the hackathon’s output has lasting value.

For competitors and investors observing LEAP 2026, the scale and output mix may sharpen interest in platforms that combine instruction, assisted building, and distribution. TechScoop analysis: if similar programs replicate the model—large cohorts, guided sprints, and a push to publish—regional ecosystems could see a rise in small, task-specific AI tools addressing local workflows. That would support Saudi Arabia’s digital transformation goals by increasing the density of practical solutions, even if many remain narrow in scope.

The numbers published by HRSD and Kanz provide a defined baseline to measure “what happens next.” Key signals to watch include how many of the 3,428 published products remain active six to 12 months on; the extent to which Saudi-based participants update or expand their builds; and whether employers begin to reference these portfolios explicitly in job postings or screening. Another marker will be whether the program’s certification structure evolves into stackable credentials with recognized outcomes, building on the joint HRSD–Lebanese American University sign-off cited by the organizers.

articles.content_html:
Mobily and Nokia sign MoU at LEAP to accelerate AI-driven networks

Saudi telecom operator Mobily and global network equipment vendor Nokia signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) at the opening day of LEAP 2026 on August 31, 2026, agreeing to work together on accelerating the deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) across wireless networks to improve performance, efficiency and sustainability. The companies said the collaboration will focus on optimizing network resource utilization, reducing operational waste, and exploring new AI-enabled services for customers — placing the initiative at the intersection of commercial network engineering and Saudi Arabia’s broader digital transformation agenda [1][2].

The MoU does not describe a fixed procurement or detailed implementation timeline, but frames a roadmap for trials, joint technical studies and proof-of-concept deployments that could inform future rollouts. Seen from the vantage of the Gulf region’s fast-evolving telecom market, the agreement represents a formalization of earlier trends: carriers increasingly look to software and AI tools to wring more capacity and energy efficiency out of existing infrastructure while preparing for next-generation services.

What AI will change in mobile networks

AI is already moving from lab experiments into production in telecom operations. In practical terms for a carrier like Mobily, AI can be applied across several network layers simultaneously. At the radio access layer, machine learning models can improve radio resource management by predicting traffic patterns and adjusting spectrum, modulation and scheduling policies in near real time. That enables higher aggregate throughput for users and better utilization of scarce radio resources during peaks and troughs.

On the transport and core network side, AI-driven traffic forecasting and anomaly detection can prioritize critical flows, accelerate fault isolation and automate routine operations that previously required human intervention. Predictive maintenance informed by equipment telemetry helps reduce unplanned outages and extends the life of active elements, while intelligent orchestration can dynamically instantiate network slices and virtual functions to meet changing service-level demands.

Energy-saving techniques are an immediate area of interest for sustainability objectives. AI models can identify underutilized cells and safely place them in low-power states, optimize cooling and power delivery across sites, or adapt beamforming and transmit power to actual user locations. The combined effect is lower energy consumption per bit delivered — a metric operators are increasingly tracking as both regulators and enterprise customers factor carbon intensity into procurement and service selection.

Beyond pure network optimization, AI unlocks new consumer and enterprise use cases. Mobily and Nokia’s agreement explicitly highlights exploring “AI-supported” services, which could include low-latency edge compute coordinated with radio scheduling for industrial IoT, enhanced location and context services for smart cities, or AI-enabled security analytics for anomaly detection. The value proposition for operators is twofold: reduce internal costs and create new revenue streams by packaging AI-enhanced connectivity with managed services.

Strategic and regional context: Vision 2030 and the MENA telecom landscape

The partnership aligns with Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030, which sets targets to diversify the economy and transform the Kingdom into a regional technology hub. Vision 2030 emphasizes digital infrastructure as a foundational element for economic diversification: large-scale cloud and data center investments, expanded fiber and 5G coverage, and policies to attract technology multinationals and startups. For national planners, intelligent networks offer a way to scale services efficiently while meeting environmental and economic targets.

Across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA), telecom operators face similar pressures. Data demand continues to grow rapidly as streaming, cloud gaming, remote work and industrial digitization expand. At the same time, capital discipline and rising energy costs push carriers to seek solutions that get more performance from existing spectrum and passive infrastructure. AI-driven network controls have become a strategic lever in this environment: they promise to increase spectral efficiency, improve customer experience metrics and lower operational expenditure.

The MoU with Nokia also reflects a broader industry dynamic in which operators balance vendor relationships and diversify technology partnerships. Mobily has previously collaborated with other vendors on radio and core network projects; this agreement with Nokia is a separate, concrete step focused specifically on AI-enabled operations and services. By testing and validating AI approaches with multiple suppliers, carriers can avoid vendor lock-in, encourage interoperability, and accelerate adoption of open frameworks such as cloud-native network functions and standardized management interfaces.

Technical implications and operational considerations

Moving from concept to fielded AI requires several technical and governance pieces to be in place. First, data availability and quality are essential: telemetry streams from radios, transport elements and customer devices must be collected, normalized and made accessible to training and inference pipelines while preserving privacy and security. Edge computing and distributed inference architectures help reduce latency for time-sensitive control loops but require careful orchestration to avoid fragmenting visibility.

Second, models must be robust to non-stationary conditions. Mobile networks experience seasonal, event-driven and geographic variability; AI systems that adjust scheduling or power settings need conservative safeguards and explainability features to ensure they do not inadvertently degrade service. Operators are therefore likely to adopt hybrid control systems that combine model-driven recommendations with rule-based policies and human oversight during early deployments.

Third, integration with existing operations support systems and business support systems is necessary for measurable impact on OPEX. AI-driven incident detection is only useful if it can trigger automated remediation or a prioritized work queue. Similarly, service-level differentiation via network slicing requires tight coordination between orchestration layers and customer billing systems.

Finally, cybersecurity and regulatory compliance will be front-of-mind. AI introduces new attack surfaces — data poisoning, adversarial inputs and model theft — so robust security engineering and continuous monitoring will be required. Regulators in the region are increasingly focused on data governance and national security considerations; partnerships that involve sensitive network controls will need clear frameworks for data residency, access and auditing.

A measured path forward typically involves staged pilots, performance metrics and published trials that quantify energy savings, latency improvements, capacity gains and customer experience lifts. The MoU’s emphasis on joint studies suggests Mobily and Nokia plan to follow that playbook, creating a body of evidence that can guide broader rollouts and regulatory discussion.

Outlook

The MoU signed at LEAP 2026 marks a formal step in a larger industry shift: AI is transitioning from an optimization adjunct to a core enabler of next-generation network functionality. For Mobily, the collaboration with Nokia offers a chance to accelerate operational modernization while aligning with Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 goals to build a competitive digital economy. For the region, successful deployments could serve as demonstrators for how AI helps operators meet rising demand with lower environmental impact. The ultimate measure will be whether pilots translate into scalable systems that deliver quantifiable improvements in efficiency, resilience and new service revenue.

articles.content_html:
During LEAP 2026, the Digital Government Authority (DGA) announced the results of Saudi Arabia's Digital Experience Maturity Index for 2026, which achieved an "Advanced" maturity level with a score of 87.06%. The announcement was made by DGA Governor Eng. Ahmed bin Mohammed Alsuwaiyan in Riyadh. The comprehensive assessment evaluated 59 digital platforms, an increase from the 50 platforms assessed in 2025. The evaluation process was rooted in four primary perspectives designed to measure effectiveness and user satisfaction comprehensively. These pillars included beneficiary satisfaction, user experience, complaints handling, and the underlying technologies and tools driving the platforms. Over 805,500 people participated in the "Evaluate Your Digital Experience" survey, a significant increase from 374,000 the previous year. The expanded scope of the survey allows for a granular understanding of user behavior and preferences, providing the DGA with a dataset to identify areas requiring attention within the public sector.

The results of the 2026 index highlight the progression in how citizens and residents interact with public platforms. The assessment methodology ensures that the maturity index reflects technological adoption and the quality of service experienced by end-users. The surge in survey participation indicates public interest and reliance on digital channels for government interactions. By establishing benchmarks, the DGA aims to ensure that public services remain responsive and accessible. The integration of platforms into the evaluation process requires ongoing investment in technology and user-centric design to maintain current maturity levels. The DGA's focus on expanding evaluation criteria and increasing public participation in future surveys will be critical in identifying areas for enhancement. Addressing challenges such as cybersecurity threats and data privacy concerns will be essential in maintaining public trust and ensuring the long-term success of the digital transformation agenda.

Platform Rankings and Performance

Among the 59 platforms evaluated, the Absher platform topped the rankings with a score of 94.38%. This ranking reflects Absher's role in facilitating essential government services for citizens and expatriates. Closely following was Etimad, which secured the second position with a score of 94.36%. The performance of these platforms indicates reliability and user satisfaction in key administrative and financial service areas. Other notable platforms that demonstrated maturity included Senaei (92.83%), Balady (92.56%), and Tawakkalna (92.50%). The performance of these core platforms demonstrates the effectiveness of investment in digital capabilities and user experience optimization. By prioritizing interactions and navigation, these platforms have set a standard for digital service delivery.

The evaluation process for the digital experience measured effectiveness and user satisfaction. The four primary perspectives—beneficiary satisfaction, user experience, complaints handling, and technologies and tools—provided a comprehensive overview of the digital landscape. The increase in the number of evaluated platforms from 50 to 59 demonstrates an expanding scope of digital governance and service delivery. The results emphasize the focus on user-centric design and the continuous refinement of digital interfaces to meet the evolving needs of the population. The data collected from the "Evaluate Your Digital Experience" survey provides insights into user preferences and pain points, enabling targeted interventions to enhance the overall digital ecosystem. The DGA's commitment to continuous improvement is reflected in the rigorous assessment methodology and the expanding scope of the index.

Digital Inclusion and Strategic Context

A component of the maturity index is the Digital Inclusion sub-index, which measures the accessibility of digital services for all segments of society. In the 2026 assessment, this sub-index achieved a score of 76.98%, placing it at the "Empowered" level. This achievement reflects targeted efforts by the DGA and other government bodies to design services that accommodate persons with disabilities, the elderly, and other vulnerable groups. Ensuring digital inclusion is a fundamental aspect of the broader digital transformation strategy, aiming to leave no citizen behind as services increasingly migrate online. The focus on accessibility aligns with global best practices and highlights a commitment to equitable service delivery. By implementing inclusive design principles and conducting rigorous accessibility testing, the government aims to bridge the digital divide and ensure that all individuals can participate in the digital economy.

The rise in the Digital Experience Maturity Index 2026 aligns with the objectives of Saudi Vision 2030. The strategic framework emphasizes the development of a vibrant society and an ambitious nation, with digital transformation serving as a key enabler. By improving the digital experience, Saudi Arabia is streamlining government operations, fostering a business-friendly environment, and improving the overall quality of life for its residents. The progress reported at LEAP 2026 solidifies the Kingdom's global position in digital government, showcasing an approach to adopting emerging technologies and refining service delivery models. The integration of advanced analytics, artificial intelligence, and cloud computing into public sector operations has been instrumental in driving these improvements, enabling more personalized and efficient service delivery. The ongoing commitment to digital excellence is expected to attract further investment and innovation, reinforcing the Kingdom's status as a leading digital economy in the region.

Assessment Methodology and Future Outlook

The comprehensive assessment for the 2026 index evaluated 59 digital platforms across four main perspectives. The increase from 50 platforms in 2025 demonstrates an expanding scope of digital governance. articles.content_html:
The data solutions and business empowerment firm Masdar has confirmed its participation as a Gold Sponsor at LEAP 2026, the technology exhibition running in Riyadh from August 31 to September 3, 2026. The company is set to showcase a comprehensive suite of data, artificial intelligence, system integration, and compliance solutions designed to support Saudi Vision 2030's digital transformation goals. This strategic move highlights the growing importance of indigenous technological capabilities in driving the Kingdom's ambitious economic diversification agenda, as outlined in the national vision.

As regional enterprises and government entities accelerate their modernization efforts, the demand for unified data platforms and automated customer interaction tools has intensified significantly over the past few years. Masdar's exhibition strategy at the prominent tech gathering focuses on providing smart infrastructure to various business sectors, positioning its product portfolio as a key enabler for digital operations in Saudi Arabia and the broader Gulf region. The company's presence as a Gold Sponsor underscores its intent to capture a larger share of the enterprise software market, which is experiencing rapid expansion driven by government mandates and private sector innovation.

Unified Data and Integration Platforms

A central component of Masdar's presentation at the Riyadh conference is "Mofeed," a unified data services platform tailored specifically for the financial technology, insurance, and government sectors. The platform aims to streamline data access, integration, and processing for organizations operating in highly regulated environments where accuracy, security, and real-time availability are critical operational imperatives. By consolidating data services into a single cohesive architecture, Mofeed is positioned to reduce operational friction and technical debt for institutions navigating complex compliance requirements and vast data volumes.

Alongside the Mofeed platform, the company will highlight "Aamaly," a specialized solution engineered for human resources and social insurance integration. The platform addresses a common and persistent administrative bottleneck for regional businesses by bridging the gap between internal HR management systems and external government social insurance frameworks. This seamless integration capability is expected to simplify workforce administration, reduce manual data entry errors, and ensure continuous compliance with evolving labor regulations, thereby allowing organizations to focus on core business activities rather than administrative overhead.

The development of these targeted platforms reflects a deep understanding of the local regulatory and business landscape. By addressing specific pain points in data management and HR integration, Masdar is providing practical tools that can yield immediate efficiency gains for its clients. The focus on interoperability and unified services is particularly relevant as organizations seek to break down data silos and create more agile operational models.

Artificial Intelligence and Compliance Focus

In the rapidly evolving customer service domain, Masdar is introducing "Labeeb," an artificial intelligence-powered customer interaction management platform. The system is designed to automate, analyze, and enhance customer engagement processes across multiple channels, allowing organizations to scale their support operations effectively while maintaining, or even improving, service quality. The deployment of sophisticated AI in customer interaction reflects a broader industry trend toward intelligent automation, particularly in sectors such as telecommunications, banking, and retail, which handle high volumes of user inquiries on a daily basis.

The company's strategic focus on regulatory adherence and sector-specific requirements is further demonstrated by the Health Insurance Compliance (HIP) platform. As the healthcare sector in Saudi Arabia undergoes significant digital transformation, driven by initiatives to improve patient outcomes and operational efficiency, tools that facilitate strict compliance with health insurance mandates are becoming increasingly essential for healthcare providers, insurers, and regulatory bodies alike. The HIP platform is structured to support these diverse stakeholders in meeting complex regulatory standards efficiently, minimizing the risk of non-compliance penalties and administrative delays.

These AI and compliance solutions demonstrate a proactive approach to technological development, anticipating the needs of industries that are undergoing rapid digitization. By embedding compliance into the core architecture of its platforms, Masdar is offering solutions that not only improve operational efficiency but also mitigate regulatory risks, a critical consideration for enterprises operating in the modern digital economy.

Strategic Alignment and Market Implications

Abdulrahim Al-Zahrani, Executive General Manager of Products at Masdar, emphasized the company's unwavering commitment to enabling digital transformation in direct alignment with Saudi Vision 2030. According to Al-Zahrani, the primary objective is to provide robust, smart infrastructure to various business sectors, thereby actively supporting the national agenda for economic diversification, technological advancement, and the creation of a knowledge-based economy. His remarks underscore the strategic alignment between Masdar's product roadmap and the broader goals of the Kingdom.

The introduction of these specialized, purpose-built platforms at LEAP 2026 indicates a strategic focus on sector-specific solutions rather than generalized, one-size-fits-all enterprise software. By targeting key verticals such as fintech, insurance, government, and healthcare, Masdar is directly addressing distinct operational challenges within industries that are central to the region's long-term economic development plans. This targeted approach allows the company to deliver higher value and more relevant functionality to its prospective clients.

While the product announcements provide a clear and compelling view of Masdar's technological direction and strategic priorities, the company has not yet detailed specific adoption metrics, pricing models, or precise deployment timelines for the showcased platforms. The market response and feedback gathered at the conference will likely influence the subsequent rollout phases, feature enhancements, and integration strategies for Mofeed, Aamaly, Labeeb, and the HIP platform across the target sectors in the coming months. The success of these platforms will ultimately depend on their ability to deliver measurable return on investment and seamless integration into existing enterprise architectures.

articles.content_html:
RIYADH — In a significant step toward digitalizing Saudi Arabia’s engineering and construction sector, the Saudi Council of Engineers has officially launched the "Mu'tamad" platform. The announcement was made during LEAP 2026 by the council's Secretary-General, Musaed bin Abdullah Al-Otaibi. Designed as an integrated digital ecosystem, Mu'tamad aims to organize, develop, and enhance the reliability of engineering and construction transactions across the Kingdom, beginning with an initial rollout in Jeddah before expanding nationwide. The launch of the platform is a a reflection of the ongoing digital transformation efforts within the Saudi engineering sector, which are essential for supporting the country's ambitious infrastructure and development goals. The Saudi Council of Engineers has positioned the Mu'tamad platform as a central hub for engineering services, aiming to streamline operations, ensure compliance with national standards, and foster a more transparent and efficient marketplace for both service providers and clients.

The platform represents a major regulatory and operational shift for the Saudi engineering landscape. According to the Saudi Council of Engineers, Mu'tamad is projected to govern over 200,000 engineering and construction transactions. By creating a centralized digital environment, the initiative seeks to bring large-scale transparency and efficiency to a sector that is foundational to the country's ongoing infrastructure and development projects. The launch underscores a broader national commitment to digital transformation and e-government services, aligning with the strategic objectives of the Saudi Digital Economy. The scale of the Mu'tamad platform is substantial, reflecting the sheer volume of engineering and construction activity currently underway in Saudi Arabia. The governance of over 200,000 transactions through a single digital platform will provide the Saudi Council of Engineers with unparalleled oversight and data on the sector's performance, enabling more informed regulatory decisions and policy adjustments in the future. This level of digitalization is expected to significantly reduce the administrative burden on both the council and the engineering firms operating within its jurisdiction, allowing them to focus more on project delivery and innovation.

Streamlining Engineering Services

At its core, the Mu'tamad platform is built to connect more than 4,000 engineering and construction service providers with clients and stakeholders. This extensive network will facilitate a range of essential functions designed to streamline project lifecycles. Key features of the platform include advanced service provider search capabilities, comprehensive contract management tools, and systems for quote comparison. These functionalities are expected to significantly reduce the friction traditionally associated with sourcing and managing engineering services in the region. The ability for clients to easily search for and compare service providers based on verified credentials and past performance will foster a more competitive and transparent market. Furthermore, the integrated contract management tools will help standardize agreements, reducing the likelihood of disputes and ensuring that both parties are clearly aligned on project deliverables and timelines. The inclusion of quote comparison systems will also empower clients to make more informed financial decisions, potentially driving down costs and improving the overall value of engineering services in the Kingdom.

Furthermore, the platform introduces rigorous digital verification processes. Mu'tamad is engineered to verify compliance against more than 4,000 design requirements based on the Saudi Building Code. This automated compliance checking is a critical component of the platform, ensuring that all governed transactions meet stringent national standards for safety, quality, and structural integrity. By digitizing these checks, the Saudi Council of Engineers aims to minimize human error and accelerate the approval phases of construction projects, which are often subject to complex regulatory scrutiny. The integration of the Saudi Building Code into the platform's verification processes is a particularly noteworthy feature. It ensures that all engineering designs and construction plans adhere to the latest safety and quality standards, which is crucial for protecting public safety and ensuring the long-term durability of the Kingdom's infrastructure. The automated nature of these checks will also significantly reduce the time required for project approvals, which has traditionally been a bottleneck in the construction process. This increased efficiency will benefit both service providers and clients, enabling projects to move from the design phase to construction more quickly and smoothly.

Economic Impact and Future Expansion

The financial implications of the Mu'tamad platform are substantial. The Saudi Council of Engineers anticipates that the digital ecosystem will generate operational savings exceeding 14 million riyals. These savings are expected to stem from increased process efficiency, reduced administrative overhead, and faster turnaround times for project approvals and compliance verifications. For the thousands of service providers operating within the Kingdom, the platform promises a more equitable and transparent marketplace, potentially lowering the barriers to entry for qualified firms and fostering healthy competition. The projected operational savings of over 14 million riyals highlight the significant economic benefits of digitalizing the engineering and construction sector. These savings can be reinvested into the sector, supporting further innovation and development. Additionally, the increased efficiency and transparency brought about by the platform will likely attract more investment into the Saudi engineering market, both from domestic and international sources. A more streamlined and reliable regulatory environment is a key factor for investors, and the Mu'tamad platform is a strong signal that the Saudi Council of Engineers is committed to creating a business-friendly ecosystem.

While the platform's initial deployment is focused on Jeddah, the phased rollout strategy indicates a careful approach to scaling this critical infrastructure. Expanding the system kingdom-wide will require robust technical support and user adoption campaigns to ensure that both service providers and clients can effectively navigate the new digital environment. The success of the Jeddah pilot will likely inform the subsequent phases of the rollout, providing valuable data on system performance and user engagement. As the platform matures, it will be closely watched by industry observers as a benchmark for digital regulatory compliance in the Middle East. The decision to launch the platform initially in Jeddah allows the Saudi Council of Engineers to test the system in a major urban center with a high volume of engineering and construction activity. This phased approach will enable the council to identify and address any technical or operational issues before rolling the platform out to the rest of the Kingdom. The lessons learned from the Jeddah deployment will be invaluable for ensuring a smooth and successful nationwide launch. The ultimate goal of the Mu'tamad platform is to create a fully integrated and digitalized engineering sector across Saudi Arabia, supporting the Kingdom's broader economic and development objectives. As the platform expands and evolves, it has the potential to become a model for other countries in the region seeking to modernize their regulatory frameworks and improve the efficiency of their engineering and construction industries.

articles.content_html:
Saudi Arabia’s Social Development Bank (SDB) announced the launch of its AI-powered “Smart Collection” service and the “Noura” smart assistant chatbot during the Saudi Digital Exhibition at LEAP 2026. The announcement marks a shift in how the public financial institution handles routine interactions and debt recovery, moving away from uniform manual outreach toward automated, data-driven systems. According to the bank’s statement, the Smart Collection system applies automated data analysis to tailor communications in its collection processes. Simultaneously, the Noura chatbot is already in use by more than one million beneficiaries and is handling roughly half of the bank’s service interactions. The presentation at LEAP 2026 framed the rollouts as part of SDB’s digital transformation and its adoption of AI to enhance customer experience and operational efficiency in the financial sector. The announcement focused on two concrete points that can be verified from the bank’s statement: the operational deployment of both systems, and the reported usage metrics for the Noura chatbot. The AI Smart Collection system analyzes customer data to personalize communication and improve collection efficiency across multiple channels, offering accurate and proactive interactions. The Noura chatbot aims to facilitate access to SDB services, demonstrating a concrete application of conversational AI within the Saudi public financial sector. LEAP’s Saudi Digital Exhibition served as the stage for that disclosure. As a major technology forum in Riyadh, LEAP brings together public institutions, private vendors and international attendees, creating a concentrated environment for governments and banks to showcase new digital services. Announcements made in that context can accelerate peer discussion, attract vendor interest and invite scrutiny from regulators and civil society. Exhibitions like this also function as a marketplace for procurement conversations, partnerships and demonstrations that can influence how quickly tools move from pilot stage to broader deployment across the Saudi digital economy.

Operational deployment and integration

The deployment of the Smart Collection service and the Noura chatbot represents a significant step in SDB's digital transformation. By analyzing customer data, the Smart Collection service aims to personalize communication strategies across multiple channels, improving collection efficiency. This involves using customer profiles and payment histories to prioritize accounts and adapt messages to the likelihood of a response. These techniques aim to improve contact rates and reduce unnecessary friction for customers interacting with the bank's collection department. The Noura chatbot's reported usage by over one million beneficiaries indicates a substantial shift of routine service interactions to an automated interface. With 50% of the bank's services being completed through Noura, SDB is demonstrating a clear reliance on natural language processing to interpret user queries and route routine requests. This shift allows staff to focus on nonstandard cases that require human intervention. However, it also raises operational questions about handoffs, oversight, and the design of escalation paths when automation cannot resolve an issue. Integrating predictive contact systems and chatbots requires robust implementation. Practical requirements include clear routing rules, ongoing calibration of the communication strategies, and continuous monitoring of contact outcomes. Human-in-the-loop controls are crucial for edge cases, and rollback mechanisms should exist if the automated systems begin to degrade in performance. Equally important is the seamless linking of automated channels to human workflows so that a customer who starts with the Noura chatbot receives consistent and up-to-date assistance when transferred to a live representative.

Automation impact on service delivery

Announcements of AI deployments by public financial institutions invite scrutiny in several operational areas. First, data governance is critical. The collection and use of personal and financial data for the Smart Collection service must comply with applicable privacy rules and the organization’s own policies. Effective governance covers data lineage, access controls, retention policies and consent management. Institutions must also monitor data quality, as incomplete datasets can skew the personalization of communication strategies or result in inconsistent treatment of beneficiaries. Second, transparency and accountability are necessary for public-facing automated systems. For collection systems, regulators and customer advocates expect clear documentation about how communication decisions are made, and mechanisms for customers to query automated outcomes. For conversational systems like Noura, audit trails that capture which decisions were made by automation and which by humans are important for resolving disputes and for ongoing system improvement. Explaining decisions in user-facing terms is part of responsible deployment, especially in services funded or overseen by public actors. Third, measurement and validation of the reported metrics require ongoing attention. The reported usage metric of one million beneficiaries and a 50% service completion rate for the Noura chatbot are useful early indicators of adoption. However, institutions moving to AI-driven workflows need to monitor changes over time, including unintended side effects like increased call-backs or confusion among certain customer segments. Continuous validation typically includes statistical monitoring of system outputs against known outcomes to ensure the automation is delivering the intended efficiency without compromising service quality.

Implementation questions and next steps

The long-term effectiveness of SDB's AI tools depends on continuous engineering, governance and independent evaluation. Public reporting of performance metrics, privacy safeguards and escalation procedures enhances public understanding and regulatory oversight, helping ensure that efficiency gains translate into fair, transparent and accountable public fintech services. The bank did not publish detailed technical specifications, performance targets, or a full timetable for wider rollout in the material released at the event, leaving these operational details as the next logical area for disclosure. As the Social Development Bank expands its automated capabilities, observers will look for evidence that the reported adoption figures are matched by clear operating safeguards and measurable service outcomes.

articles.content_html:
RIYADH — Microsoft has officially confirmed that its Saudi Arabia East datacentre region will launch in November 2026, delivering local cloud and artificial intelligence infrastructure to the Kingdom. The announcement, highlighted by Ayman Alghamdi at LEAP 2026, is a step for data residency and compliance, allowing highly regulated sectors like banking and government to transition mission-critical AI workloads to Azure.

Located in the Eastern Province, the facility features three Azure Availability Zones designed for high availability and low latency. This development aligns with Saudi Arabia's broader digital transformation goals and is projected to generate substantial economic value and local job creation. The confirmation solidifies Microsoft's commitment to the region amid growing competition in the cloud infrastructure space [1].

The establishment of the Saudi Arabia East cloud region represents a strategic investment in the Middle East's rapidly expanding digital economy. By providing localized data processing and storage capabilities, Microsoft addresses the stringent regulatory requirements of public sector entities and financial institutions. These organizations can now leverage advanced artificial intelligence and machine learning tools without compromising on data sovereignty mandates. The availability of enterprise-grade cloud services within the country's borders is expected to accelerate the adoption of innovative technologies across various industries, fostering a more resilient and competitive business environment.

Infrastructure and Availability Zones

The new cloud region in the Eastern Province is designed to deliver robust performance and reliability. The inclusion of three Azure Availability Zones ensures that mission-critical applications remain operational even in the event of localized failures. Each zone consists of one or more datacentres equipped with independent power, cooling, and networking infrastructure. This architecture provides high availability and low latency, which are essential for supporting high-density AI and enterprise workloads. The deployment of these advanced facilities underscores Microsoft's dedication to providing state-of-the-art cloud solutions that meet the demanding needs of modern businesses and government agencies.

The Eastern Province is a major hub for energy and industrial activities, making it an ideal location for a facility that requires significant power and connectivity resources. The proximity to key economic centers also ensures that organizations across the Kingdom can benefit from low-latency access to cloud services. This localized approach not only improves performance but also helps to mitigate the risks associated with data transmission over long distances. As a result, businesses can operate more efficiently and securely, driving further growth and innovation in the region.

The integration of advanced security measures and compliance certifications will provide customers with the confidence they need to migrate sensitive workloads to the cloud. Furthermore, the region's architecture is designed to support the seamless integration of hybrid cloud environments, enabling organizations to maintain existing on-premises infrastructure while leveraging the scalability and flexibility of the public cloud. This hybrid approach is particularly beneficial for large enterprises with complex IT requirements and legacy systems that cannot be easily transitioned to a fully cloud-native architecture.

Economic Impact and Job Creation

The launch of the Saudi Arabia East cloud region is anticipated to have a profound impact on the local economy. According to an IDC study, the new infrastructure will contribute an estimated $44 billion in new revenues for the Saudi economy between 2027 and 2030. This substantial economic boost will be driven by the increased productivity and efficiency of businesses that adopt cloud technologies, as well as the growth of the local technology ecosystem. The availability of advanced cloud services will also attract foreign investment, further stimulating economic development and diversification.

In addition to the financial benefits, the project is expected to create around 100,000 jobs across the Kingdom. These employment opportunities will span various sectors, including IT, engineering, construction, and operations. The influx of new jobs will not only reduce unemployment but also help to build a highly skilled workforce capable of supporting the country's digital transformation initiatives. Microsoft's investment in local talent development and training programs will further enhance the capabilities of the Saudi workforce, ensuring that the Kingdom remains competitive in the global digital economy. The long-term economic and social benefits of the cloud region will be felt for years to come.

The economic multiplier effect of the cloud region extends beyond direct job creation and revenue generation. The development of a robust local technology ecosystem will foster innovation and entrepreneurship, leading to the creation of new startups and digital businesses. articles.content_html:
Riyadh — Saudi Arabia’s General Directorate of Passports has launched a digital service that lets residents update their personal photos directly through the Absher app, removing the need to visit a passport office. The update, aimed at expatriate residents, is accessible via Absher’s “My Workers” section and is part of the Kingdom’s ongoing expansion of e-government services, the agency confirmed in an announcement carried by local media [1]. For users, the change turns what was a time-consuming errand into a task that can be completed on a phone.

The move matters because photo updates sit at the core of identity management for residents navigating day-to-day services. By shifting the process into an established national platform, authorities are tackling a recurring administrative hurdle while reducing foot traffic at passport offices. The practical result is less disruption for workers and employers, and a freer hand for government counters to concentrate on cases that cannot be handled online [1][2].

How the photo update works on Absher

The General Directorate of Passports said residents can submit a new personal photo through the Absher mobile app in the “My Workers” section, which serves as the gateway for this task [1]. While the agency did not publish a step-by-step guide alongside the announcement, the placement inside Absher indicates the feature is intended to sit with routine residency administration, making it reachable for the expatriate audience that already uses the platform for official tasks.

Importantly, the update is framed as a substitute for an in-person visit. Previously, changing the photo tied to a residency record required scheduling an appointment and attending a passport office during working hours. In a country with a large expatriate workforce, those visits add up, often resulting in workday interruptions and added coordination for employers. Moving the submission into Absher removes that scheduling friction and centralizes the task in a single digital channel [1].

The agency’s framing also suggests the service is designed to meet official record-keeping needs without introducing new steps or separate portals. By anchoring the process in Absher, authorities can rely on an app residents already recognize, and they can update records within the same digital identity framework that underpins other public services in the Kingdom [1][2].

Why the change matters for residents and employers

For expatriate residents, the biggest gain is predictability. Updating a personal photo is no longer tied to office hours or appointment availability, meaning workers can complete the requirement from a phone at a time that suits them. That cuts down on commuting, waiting times, and lost productivity tied to midweek appointments. It also limits the risk of delays in keeping records current, which can affect everyday interactions that depend on a valid, up-to-date identity photo.

Employers also stand to benefit. Companies that sponsor expatriate workers typically coordinate administrative tasks governed by the General Directorate of Passports. A self-service option inside Absher reduces the back-and-forth that can arise when multiple employees need to update records at once. It also lowers the number of permission letters, appointment confirmations, or physical check-ins managers have to track when employees are pulled away for government visits.

On the public sector side, the change can ease pressure at branch counters. When a high-volume task like photo updates moves online, front-line staff can redirect time to edge cases that truly require in-person handling—complex status changes, exceptional documentation, or issues that demand manual review. In a digital government setting, such triaging is key to sustaining service levels while expanding the menu of online options [1].

Context: an Absher-led push to simplify routine admin

Absher has emerged as the default entry point for Saudi government e-services, and the photo update feature is another example of authorities funneling routine resident interactions into one protected channel. The approach is consistent with digital transformation themes regularly showcased at major Saudi technology events, including LEAP 2026, where concrete, user-facing improvements are emphasized over abstract plans [1]. In this case, the emphasis is on a specific fix to a common pain point: aligning identity photos with current records without forcing a trip to a government office.

While the announcement did not enumerate technical underpinnings, anchoring the feature in Absher signals a priority for continuity and trust. Residents have a central login, a standard interface, and a unified history of submissions. Authorities, meanwhile, gain a single pipeline for receiving updates tied to identity records, which typically simplifies auditing and reduces fragmentation across departments. Supporting coverage indicates this rollout is part of a broader stream of Absher enhancements designed to keep routine services moving online [2].

For investors and technology firms watching the Saudi market, the takeaway is straightforward: the government continues to migrate discrete, high-friction tasks to digital workflows when doing so preserves security and improves user experience. Each service that crosses that threshold increases the stickiness of the national platform and sets expectations for further consolidation of tasks residents once handled in person.

What’s unclear and what to watch

The announcement leaves several operational details for the rollout to clarify. The General Directorate of Passports did not publish photo specifications such as resolution, background color, file format, or framing guidelines within the initial notice. Processing times—how quickly a newly uploaded photo is reflected across integrated systems—were also not listed. Residents will likely encounter these requirements within the Absher interface as they submit updates, but they were not enumerated in the public summary [1].

TechScoop analysis: As usage ramps up, two tests will define how smooth the transition feels. First, the clarity of in-app prompts and error handling—residents need to know instantly if a photo meets criteria or requires resubmission. Second, the handoff from upload to record update—if changes propagate consistently and predictably, confidence in the digital path will rise and further reduce foot traffic at passport offices. Both areas are common pressure points when physical procedures go digital, and both are solvable with strong interface cues and steady back-end performance.

More broadly, this release creates a template for where authorities could go next: routine identity maintenance delivered in-app, and a diminishing need for residents to book appointment slots for standard updates. The agency did not attach a roadmap or commit to additional features in its announcement, so expectations beyond the photo-update use case should be treated as speculative until the Directorate provides further detail [1][2].

For now, the significance lies in what has already changed. A task tied to identity verification—historically one of the more conservative corners of public administration—has moved fully online for Saudi Arabia’s expatriate residents. The direction of travel is clear even if the next milestones are not: fewer counters, more screens, and a tighter loop between residents and the records they are responsible for keeping current.

  2. Supporting coverage on Absher updates

articles.content_html:
The Saudi General Directorate of Civil Defense is using LEAP 2026 to put public safety technology at the center of a national digital transformation story. Participating as a strategic sponsor under the Ministry of Interior’s pavilion, the directorate is presenting its work from August 31 to September 3, 2026, under the theme “Technical Solutions for a Safe Nation.” The showcase highlights three pillars of its digital services and safety technologies: a Smart Helmet for frontline operations, the National Early Warning Platform for emergencies, and the electronic Salama portal. Together, these tools signal a coordinated push to enhance public safety, improve incident response efficiency, and protect lives and property.

A strategic public safety showcase

Civil Defense’s role as a strategic sponsor under the Ministry of Interior pavilion underscores how Saudi public safety agencies are aligning technology adoption with national priorities. The “Technical Solutions for a Safe Nation” theme frames safety not as a standalone function but as an integrated outcome of prevention, preparedness, and rapid response. By situating its showcase within the Ministry of Interior’s ecosystem, the directorate highlights how countering risk requires collaboration across agencies and platforms, from early alerts to on‑scene operations.

This positioning matters for two reasons. First, it puts practical emergency-management capabilities—not just broad digital ambitions—into the spotlight. Rather than a generic presence at a technology fair, Civil Defense is anchoring its participation in specific tools it is deploying. Second, it connects the dots between policy and practice. Public safety outcomes depend on how quickly information moves, how clearly it is communicated, and how effectively responders are equipped. The selected technologies speak directly to those levers.

What the Civil Defense is exhibiting

The Smart Helmet represents the operational edge of the directorate’s technology push. As a specialized piece of safety equipment, it is designed to support responders in hazardous conditions and to strengthen on‑scene effectiveness. Its inclusion in the LEAP 2026 lineup signals attention to the needs of personnel who confront emergencies directly, reinforcing the principle that protecting responders is foundational to protecting the public.

The National Early Warning Platform anchors the preventive side of the portfolio. Early warning is one of the most consequential capabilities in emergency management because it can change behavior before harm escalates. By spotlighting a dedicated platform for emergency alerts, Civil Defense emphasizes the value of timely, authoritative notifications that help people and organizations take protective action. Whether the incident is fast-moving or slow-building, the ability to issue clear, structured warnings and guidance can reduce confusion, improve compliance with safety instructions, and limit exposure to risk.

The Salama electronic portal rounds out the directorate’s focus on digital services. As an online gateway for safety-related processes and services, it is designed to centralize interactions and documentation that underpin safer environments. Digitization in this domain can shorten processing times, improve transparency, and make safety requirements easier to understand and follow. By spotlighting Salama, the directorate points to a continuous, everyday layer of safety work that complements emergency response: establishing clear standards, making them accessible, and ensuring that safety practices are embedded before incidents occur.

While the three tools occupy different parts of the safety lifecycle—preparedness and prevention, operational response, and service delivery—they share a common aim. Each is intended to move information faster and more reliably to the people who need it, when they need it. That focus on timeliness and clarity is the connective tissue that links the technologies to their ultimate purpose: safeguarding lives and property.

Why it matters for response and resilience

The Civil Defense’s LEAP 2026 showcase conveys several implications for how the Kingdom approaches risk, readiness, and recovery.

First, it emphasizes that faster, clearer information saves time—and time saves lives. The National Early Warning Platform is a direct investment in compressing the gap between detecting a threat and informing the public about what to do next. Even small improvements in the speed and clarity of alerts can reduce exposure, limit secondary incidents, and help responders concentrate resources where they are needed most.

Second, it shows that frontline safety is a technology priority, not an afterthought. By putting a Smart Helmet on the exhibit floor, the directorate is sending a message that operational gear is part of the digital public safety equation. Equipping responders with specialized tools can help them work more safely and efficiently under pressure, which in turn supports faster containment of incidents and reduces the likelihood of cascading harm.

Third, it recognizes that prevention is an everyday, digital service. The Salama portal addresses the essential but often overlooked dimension of safety: routine processes that keep people, facilities, and activities within safe parameters before emergencies happen. Digitally accessible services can make it easier to understand and meet safety obligations, reducing friction for users and helping the directorate apply standards consistently. Over time, that consistency can lower the baseline risk the public faces.

Finally, the showcase reflects an integrated approach. Housing these technologies under the Ministry of Interior’s pavilion reinforces the idea that effective incident management is a team sport. Early warnings are more useful when they align with field operations; operational tools are more effective when responders and the public share a common operating picture; and safety services are more impactful when they are part of an end‑to‑end system rather than standalone applications. Interoperability, governance, and coordinated procedures are therefore as important as the devices and platforms themselves.

The public interest case is straightforward. When warnings reach people promptly, when responders are better protected and supported, and when safety processes are digitally streamlined, incident response becomes more efficient and outcomes improve. That means fewer preventable injuries, less property damage, and quicker paths to recovery. It also builds trust: the public is more likely to act on guidance from institutions that demonstrate competence and clarity during high‑stakes moments.

LEAP 2026 provides a high-visibility proof point for this direction of travel. The Civil Defense’s selection of the Smart Helmet, the National Early Warning Platform, and the Salama portal signals a balanced investment across the safety lifecycle. It aligns with the event’s theme by focusing on concrete capabilities rather than abstract concepts, and it frames technology as a means to an end: protecting people and property.

The work ahead will focus on making these tools work together directly, ensuring they are widely accessible, and continuously refining how they are used. That includes practicing how warnings are crafted and disseminated, ensuring frontline teams can get the most from their equipment, and keeping digital services clear and reliable. The directorate’s presence as a strategic sponsor underscores that this is not a side project—it is core to how the Kingdom intends to strengthen public safety. As LEAP 2026 runs from August 31 to September 3, the message is clear: building a safer nation increasingly depends on smart, integrated public safety technologies that translate strategy into everyday capability.

The participation of the Saudi Border Guard at LEAP 2026 highlights the intersection of national security and digital innovation. The introduction of the Zawal portal carries practical implications for the future of Saudi border control. By deploying this technology, the Saudi Border Guard is positioned to improve its regulatory operations, potentially setting a new standard for maritime security in the Gulf Region. The focus on enhancing efficiency suggests that the portal will facilitate faster and more reliable data processing, which is critical for effective border management. TechScoop analysis indicates that this focus on efficiency is a common driver for public-sector technology adoption, as agencies seek to optimize resource allocation and improve response times.

While the announcement outlines the intended benefits of the Zawal portal, it leaves certain material questions unanswered regarding the specific technical capabilities and the timeline for full implementation across all maritime borders. As the deployment progresses, further information will be required to assess the long-term impact of this digital transformation on the Saudi Border Guard's operational readiness. Strategic Importance in the Region

The unveiling of the Zawal portal at LEAP 2026 also underscores the strategic importance of maritime security in the Gulf Region. As a critical hub for global logistics and supply chains, the region requires robust border control mechanisms to ensure the safe and efficient movement of goods and people. The Saudi Border Guard's initiative to enhance maritime security through advanced technological solutions aligns with the broader regional objectives of maintaining stability and facilitating trade. The deployment of the Zawal portal is a proactive measure to address the evolving challenges of border management in a highly dynamic environment.

By leveraging digital government solutions, the Ministry of Interior is demonstrating its commitment to modernizing national security infrastructure. articles.content_html:
Muslim-first technology brand iQIBLA announced its debut at the LEAP 2026 exhibition in Riyadh, introducing a new ecosystem strategy alongside three distinct product lines. The launch, which runs from August 31 to September 3, represents a material expansion for the company beyond its established smart prayer rings. Central to the announcement are the Zikr Ring R1 and the diamond-set Aura series, marking an evolution in the brand's core hardware portfolio. In a separate push into health tracking and family electronics, the company introduced the Hajj Band—a smart wristband engineered to monitor pilgrim health and safety during Hajj and Umrah—as well as a blood pressure smartwatch tailored for Muslim users. The third pillar of the debut involves the Qimi AI product line, which features the QIMI Phone, described by the company as the world's first smartphone designed for Muslim children, alongside the QIMI Watch K2s. This distinct hardware focus highlights the intersection of religious practice and modern consumer electronics, offering a concrete product launch story that avoids general event overviews or infrastructure announcements. The ecosystem is designed to integrate smart hardware, software services, and artificial intelligence specifically for Muslim life scenarios.

Advancing Faith-Based Wearables

The introduction of the Zikr Ring R1 and the Aura series faith jewelry demonstrates a targeted approach to the niche market of Islamic faith tech. The company has built its early reputation on practical utility, and these new rings aim to maintain that functionality while elevating the aesthetic appeal. The Aura series, in particular, incorporates diamond settings, indicating an effort to capture a higher-end consumer segment that values both religious observance and premium design. By launching these products at a major technology exhibition in Saudi Arabia, iQIBLA is positioning itself within a key demographic center for its target audience. The devices are engineered to directly integrate faith into daily routines, providing users with functional pieces of smart jewelry. This expansion reflects the brand's strategy to create products that resonate with the cultural and religious values of its user base while appealing to a broader market interested in high-quality wearable technology. The integration of advanced sensors and connectivity features ensures that the hardware remains practical for modern consumers, blending traditional aesthetics with contemporary technology. The debut at the Riyadh tech exhibition provides a high-profile platform to introduce these hardware innovations to the regional and global market, signaling a shift toward lifestyle integration.

Expanding into Health and Pilgrim Safety

In a notable move into health and family technology, the company launched the iQIBLA Health line, anchored by the Hajj Band. This smart wristband is specifically engineered to monitor pilgrims' health and safety during Hajj and Umrah. The introduction of such a device addresses a practical, operational need for health monitoring during physically demanding religious pilgrimages. Alongside the Hajj Band, the company unveiled a blood pressure smartwatch tailored for Muslim users, further expanding its health-focused offerings. These developments indicate a broader strategy to integrate biometric tracking with faith-based routines. The Hajj Band's capability to track vital signs and provide real-time health data represents a targeted innovation for the millions of pilgrims who travel to Mecca each year. By focusing on the unique requirements of this demographic, the brand is demonstrating an understanding of its market and a commitment to providing solutions that enhance user safety and well-being. The blood pressure smartwatch complements this by offering continuous health monitoring, allowing users to keep track of their cardiovascular metrics while engaging in their daily religious practices. This move into health technology highlights the intersection of religious practice and modern consumer electronics, offering a concrete product launch story that addresses a critical need for health monitoring during physically demanding events. The operational implications for public health management during major religious gatherings could be significant if adoption reaches scale.

Introducing AI Electronics for Children

The company also unveiled the Qimi AI product line, aimed at younger demographics and Muslim children. This line features the QIMI Phone, billed by the company as the world's first smartphone designed specifically for Muslim children, and the QIMI Watch K2s. The introduction of these devices suggests an effort to build brand loyalty from an early age and provide technology solutions that align with family values and religious education. The Qimi AI line includes features that promote educational content, parental controls, and engaging activities tailored to the cultural context of its users. The QIMI Phone and QIMI Watch K2s are designed to provide a safe and enriching digital environment for children, ensuring that they can explore technology without compromising their values. articles.content_html:
Riyadh — At LEAP 2026, San Francisco-based AI infrastructure provider Together AI and Saudi Arabian enterprise HUMAIN announced a strategic partnership to construct a new 250-megawatt data center in the Kingdom. The collaboration aims to merge HUMAIN's expansive multi-chip AI infrastructure with Together AI's native cloud platform and global open-source developer ecosystem, creating a major new hub for high-performance computing in the Middle East.

The joint venture is projected to generate over $5 billion in gross annualized revenue during its first year of operation, signaling significant commercial expectations for the facility. This partnership will provide global developers and AI-native enterprises with high-performance AI infrastructure tailored for training and inference workloads deployed directly in Saudi Arabia. The announcement at LEAP 2026 highlights the growing momentum of international technology investments in the region, driven by the demand for specialized computing environments capable of supporting complex artificial intelligence applications.

Strategic Infrastructure for AI Workloads

The planned 250-megawatt facility represents a substantial addition to the region's computing capacity. By combining HUMAIN's multi-chip hardware approach with Together AI's specialized cloud software stack, the partnership seeks to offer a comprehensive environment for organizations building and deploying large-scale artificial intelligence models. The initiative aims to serve developers, enterprises, and AI-native organizations worldwide, leveraging the Kingdom's robust power capacity and strategic location for low-latency access to markets across Europe, the Middle East, and Africa.

According to the companies, the collaboration is designed to address the growing global demand for efficient and accessible AI compute resources. The integration of Together AI's platform is intended to streamline the deployment process for developers utilizing open-source AI models, while HUMAIN's infrastructure provides the necessary physical foundation and power density required for intensive machine learning tasks. This combination of hardware and software capabilities is positioned to offer a compelling alternative for enterprises seeking to optimize their AI operations outside of traditional technology hubs.

The sheer scale of the 250-megawatt deployment indicates a focus on accommodating the massive power and cooling requirements associated with modern AI accelerators. As the complexity of training foundational models increases, the availability of purpose-built facilities with sufficient energy resources has become a critical bottleneck for the industry. The Saudi Arabian location offers strategic advantages in this regard, providing the necessary infrastructure to support high-density computing at a global scale.

Building a Complete AI Value Chain

For HUMAIN, led by CEO Tareq Amin, the data center project supports a broader strategy to build a complete AI value chain within Saudi Arabia. The partnership aligns with national initiatives to position the Kingdom as a global hub for next-generation AI services and digital infrastructure. By securing advanced computing capabilities domestically, the venture aims to attract international technology companies and foster local innovation ecosystems, contributing to the broader economic diversification goals of the region.

Vipul Ved Prakash, Co-Founder and CEO of Together AI, brings the company's focus on AI-native inference and open-source ecosystems to the joint effort. The collaboration provides Together AI with a significant physical footprint in a rapidly developing market, expanding its capacity to serve international clients requiring specialized cloud environments. The partnership also reinforces the company's commitment to supporting open-source AI development by providing the necessary infrastructure for developers to train and deploy models efficiently.

The strategic alignment between the two companies reflects a broader trend of international collaboration in the AI sector. By pooling their respective expertise in hardware infrastructure and cloud software, Together AI and HUMAIN aim to create a vertically integrated solution that addresses the specific needs of AI-driven enterprises.
